summary:
During long-duration space missions, astronauts may need to assess changes in their health without immediate medical assistance from Earth. Yet an unusual reading does not necessarily indicate illness: it may reflect exercise, individual differences, unstable personal baselines, or a sensor problem.
That's why we developed HealthGuard, an interactive astronaut-health monitoring and research prototype that emphasizes not only detecting unusual changes but also explaining how reliable the available evidence is. Its Adaptive Personalized Deviation Reliability Analysis (APDRA) examines baseline sensitivity using 5,990 historical biomedical observations from NASA's Inspiration4 mission (OSD-575). Separately, a five-channel 1D-CNN autoencoder and a covariance-based detector identify unusual patterns in simulated physiological data, while PhysioAlert evaluates activity context, measurement quality, detector agreement, and persistence before generating understandable review prompts.
The application presents 17 simulated indicators (nine physiological and eight spacecraft or spacesuit engineering measures) across four fictional astronaut streams, with nine interactive mission scenarios, a Body Explorer, a Health Routine, a Health Library, and Moon and Mars suit HUD demonstrations. The expanded channels provide mission context but are not all inputs to the currently evaluated AI models.
details:
HealthGuard: An AI-Powered Physiological Monitoring, Anomaly Detection, and Health Risk Assessment System for Astronauts

HealthGuard UI Tour:

HealthGuard GitHub Link: https://github.com/Rhenzmar/HealthGuard.git

The Problem and Our Approach

Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to physiological challenges caused by microgravity, radiation, isolation, and confined environments. These conditions can affect cardiovascular function, immune responses, metabolism, and overall health. During missions to the Moon or Mars, limited medical resources and communication delays may make it difficult to obtain immediate assistance from Earth. Astronauts therefore need accessible monitoring tools that can help them recognize unusual physiological changes and understand when further assessment may be necessary.

However, detecting an unusual measurement is not the same as identifying a health problem. Physiological indicators naturally differ between individuals and can change temporarily during exercise, recovery, or environmental disturbances. Sensor errors and limited baseline observations can also produce misleading results. Conventional threshold-based monitoring may not adequately account for these factors, while AI-based anomaly detectors can identify unfamiliar patterns without necessarily explaining their significance. This creates a need for systems that consider not only whether a physiological change occurs, but also the reliability and context of the evidence supporting it.

To address these challenges, we developed HealthGuard, an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring and research platform integrating personalized biomedical analysis, deep-learning anomaly detection, and context-aware monitoring. Its Adaptive Personalized Deviation Reliability Analysis (APDRA) evaluates the consistency of physiological changes relative to individual baseline observations using historical NASA Inspiration4 biomedical data. Separately, a 1D-CNN autoencoder and covariance-based detector identify unusual patterns in simulated physiological signals, while PhysioAlert considers physical activity, sensor quality, detector agreement, and anomaly persistence before generating understandable assessments. Through interactive mission simulations, physiological visualizations, and educational tools, HealthGuard explores how astronauts could monitor their health more independently and make better-informed decisions during future space missions.

Project Overview

HealthGuard is an interactive astronaut health monitoring and research platform designed to help astronauts recognize physiological changes, understand potential health concerns, and explore how their bodies respond to different space mission conditions. The system combines AI-assisted anomaly detection, personalized biomedical research, simulated physiological monitoring, and interactive health education within one web application.

The platform presents 17 simulated physiological and engineering indicators across four independent fictional astronaut profiles. Its monitoring system uses a 1D-CNN autoencoder and covariance-based detector to analyze five core physiological signals, while additional indicators provide information about cardiovascular, respiratory, thermal, and spacecraft environmental conditions. PhysioAlert interprets monitoring results by considering measurement reliability, physical activity, and persistent abnormalities. Separately, APDRA uses historical NASA Inspiration4 biomedical observations to investigate how consistently physiological changes can be identified from individual baseline measurements.

Beyond monitoring, HealthGuard includes an interactive Body Explorer, a gamified Health Routine, an educational Health Library, a scenario-based Mission Control, and a Mission HUD demonstrating how astronauts could view monitoring information while operating in lunar and Martian environments. Together, these features create an integrated research and educational prototype for exploring more personalized, understandable, and autonomous astronaut health monitoring.

What It Does

HealthGuard brings physiological monitoring, AI-based pattern detection, personalized biomedical analysis, and mission simulations into a single interactive platform. Its main capabilities include:

1. Physiological and Environmental Monitoring

HealthGuard displays 17 simulated indicators consisting of nine physiological measures and eight spacecraft or spacesuit engineering measures. These include cardiovascular, respiratory, and temperature-related indicators alongside simulated cabin conditions, radiation exposure, and oxygen reserves. Users can select among four fictional astronauts, examine continuously updating graphs, and observe how measurements change during different mission scenarios. The existing AI models analyze five core physiological indicators, while the additional channels use separate simulation-based screening.

2. AI-Powered Anomaly Detection and PhysioAlert

HealthGuard uses a 1D-CNN autoencoder and a covariance-based statistical detector to identify unusual patterns across five simulated physiological signals. Rather than treating every unusual measurement as a medical emergency, PhysioAlert considers detector agreement, declared physical activity, measurement quality, and anomaly persistence. The system produces understandable explanations and monitoring prompts to help users distinguish ordinary activity-related changes, unreliable measurements, and patterns that may require additional investigation.

3. Personalized Biomedical Analysis through APDRA

The Adaptive Personalized Deviation Reliability Analysis (APDRA) framework examines the consistency of physiological changes relative to individual baseline observations. Using 5,990 historical biomedical observations from NASA's Inspiration4 mission, APDRA evaluates whether a screening finding remains consistent when different baseline measurements are excluded. This allows users to investigate how limited or variable personal reference data can influence the interpretation of physiological changes.

4. Interactive Health Education and Daily Routines

HealthGuard includes a 3D Body Explorer that connects physiological indicators to relevant body systems, allowing users to explore how changes may relate to human physiology. Its Health Library presents accessible health information and historical NASA biomedical findings. Meanwhile, Health Routine introduces gamified health activities, including physical exercises, daily wellness challenges, educational games, and progress tracking, encouraging astronauts to maintain healthy routines throughout their missions.

5. Mission Control and Scenario Simulation

Mission Control allows users to explore nine simulated scenarios involving physical exercise, oxygenation disturbances, temperature changes, sensor errors, CO₂ scrubber failure, cabin pressure loss, and radiation exposure. These simulations demonstrate how physiological measurements, environmental conditions, and monitoring assessments may change during different mission events. Users can examine the system's responses, explore trends, and observe how context affects the interpretation of unusual measurements.

6. Mission HUD for Moon and Mars Operations

HealthGuard includes interactive Mission HUD demonstrations designed to explore how physiological and mission-related information could appear inside an astronaut's spacesuit. Users can switch between lunar and Martian environments and view simulated health indicators, suit conditions, and mission alerts through a transparent heads-up display. The HUD illustrates how important monitoring information could remain accessible during extravehicular activities without requiring astronauts to navigate the main application.

Together, these capabilities demonstrate how HealthGuard could support more accessible, personalized, and understandable health monitoring during future space missions. Its current implementation remains a research and educational prototype using simulated live telemetry and authentic historical NASA biomedical observations, rather than a clinically validated medical system.

Current Data Sources and Proposed Sensor Integration

HealthGuard is designed to receive physiological and environmental data from wearable medical sensors, spacecraft monitoring equipment, and spacesuit telemetry systems. Rather than requiring an entirely new wearable device, the proposed system could integrate with existing space-compatible monitoring technologies.

One example is the Bio-Monitor, developed by the Canadian Space Agency, which uses a sensor-equipped smart shirt and headband to measure heart activity, breathing, blood pressure, skin temperature, oxygen saturation, and physical activity. Additional equipment, such as radiation dosimeters and spacesuit sensors, could provide environmental exposure and life-support measurements.

In the proposed operational system, these measurements would be transmitted through an onboard data interface to HealthGuard, where signals would be synchronized, checked for reliability, and analyzed by three main components:

  1. APDRA: Evaluates physiological changes relative to each astronaut's personal baseline.
  2. AI Anomaly Detection: Uses a 1D-CNN autoencoder and covariance-based analysis to identify unusual multichannel patterns.
  3. PhysioAlert: Combines detected anomalies with activity context, signal reliability, and persistence to determine alert severity.

Results would then appear on the Mission Dashboard, Crew Telemetry, and Mission HUD, allowing astronauts to recognize changes and respond appropriately.

Current prototype: HealthGuard demonstrates simulated live telemetry for four astronauts, using 17 monitoring indicators consisting of nine physiological and eight spacecraft or spacesuit engineering measures.

How It Works

HealthGuard receives simulated physiological and spacecraft telemetry, evaluates unusual patterns using its AI anomaly detectors, and uses PhysioAlert to assess whether changes persist, agree across detectors, and make sense in the astronaut's activity context. Instead of simply reporting an abnormal reading, it provides an understandable alert, recommends rechecking measurements when appropriate, and displays the result through the Mission Dashboard and suit HUD. This workflow is currently demonstrated using simulated data, with physical sensor integration proposed for future development.

1. Adaptive Personalized Deviation Reliability Analysis (APDRA)

APDRA evaluates how consistently a physiological change can be identified relative to an individual's baseline measurements. Rather than relying on a single preflight reference value, it applies a leave-one-baseline-out (LOO) procedure to examine whether a screening result changes when individual reference observations are excluded.

For each participant, the algorithm repeatedly removes one preflight measurement and recalculates the baseline median:

B₍₋ᵢ₎ = median(B \ {bᵢ})

where B represents the available baseline observations, bᵢ is the excluded measurement, and B₍₋ᵢ₎ is the recalculated reference value.

For Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) measurements, the percentage deviation is calculated as:

Dᵢ = 100 × |x − B₍₋ᵢ₎| / |B₍₋ᵢ₎|

where x represents the postflight measurement. CMP screening uses an exploratory 30% deviation threshold, while NULISA protein measurements use an absolute difference threshold of 1.0 on their log₂-normalized scale.

A finding is considered baseline-consistent when every leave-one-out comparison exceeds the applicable threshold in the same direction. Otherwise, it may be identified as baseline-sensitive, indicating that its interpretation depends on the available reference measurements.

APDRA was applied to 5,990 historical biomedical observations from NASA's Inspiration4 mission (OSD-575). Its purpose is to evaluate the stability of screening evidence, not to diagnose medical conditions. The analysis operates independently of HealthGuard's live simulation models.

2. 1D-CNN Autoencoder for Physiological Anomaly Detection

HealthGuard uses a one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1D-CNN) autoencoder to identify unusual temporal patterns in simulated physiological measurements.

The model processes five indicators: heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), respiratory rate, body temperature, and heart rate variability (HRV). Measurements are normalized relative to an initial 45-sample individual reference period before being analyzed through rolling 60-sample windows.

The autoencoder learns to reconstruct normal simulated physiological patterns. When a new sequence differs substantially from what the model has learned, its reconstruction error increases.

The reconstruction error is calculated using mean squared error:

E_CNN = (1/N) × Σ(xᵢ − x̂ᵢ)²

where xᵢ represents the original normalized measurement, x̂ᵢ represents its reconstructed value, and N = 300 represents the 60 timepoints across five physiological indicators.

When the reconstruction error exceeds a threshold calibrated using separate normal simulated episodes, the model flags the sequence as unusual. This enables HealthGuard to detect unfamiliar numerical patterns without requiring predefined labels for every possible anomaly.

3. Covariance-Based Statistical Detection

To complement the CNN, HealthGuard incorporates an independent shrinkage-covariance statistical detector that examines relationships and deviations across multiple physiological signals.

The detector extracts 20 features from each measurement window, including the mean, standard deviation, maximum absolute value, and beginning-to-end change for each of the five indicators.

It calculates a statistical novelty score:

S_cov = (1/20) × (f − μ)ᵀ P(f − μ)

where f is the extracted feature vector, μ is the learned reference mean, and P is the precision matrix derived from the shrinkage-covariance model.

While the CNN identifies unusual temporal patterns through reconstruction error, the covariance detector evaluates deviations from learned multivariable characteristics. Comparing their outputs allows HealthGuard to identify detector agreement or disagreement and provide additional context when interpreting unfamiliar physiological patterns.

4. PhysioAlert: Context-Aware Monitoring and Assessment

PhysioAlert interprets the outputs of the CNN and covariance detector alongside four contextual factors: detector agreement, declared physical activity, measurement quality, and anomaly persistence.

The system examines whether unusual measurements occur during exercise or rest, whether readings contain possible sensor artifacts, whether both detectors identify unusual patterns, and whether those patterns continue over time.

Its measurement-quality checks examine missing channels, irregular sampling, frozen signals, abrupt spikes, and other potentially unreliable observations. For persistent-pattern assessments, the implemented logic requires at least two qualifying positive detector checks separated by 15 seconds during declared rest, with a separate 60-second post-activity observation period.

Based on these conditions, PhysioAlert produces understandable assessments such as Activity Context Review, Verify Measurement Quality, Detectors Disagree, and Persistent Pattern Review. These explanations help users understand why an observation may require verification or further investigation.

The application also displays Optimal, Check, Warning, and Critical states during scripted mission simulations. These indicators illustrate monitoring and mission-response behavior rather than clinically validated emergency classifications.

5. Expanded 17-Channel Monitoring and Mission Simulation

HealthGuard expands its monitoring interface to 17 simulated indicators, consisting of nine physiological measures and eight spacecraft or spacesuit engineering measures.

The five original physiological indicators are processed by the evaluated AI models. Four additional physiological indicators, including blood-pressure measurements, skin temperature, and end-tidal CO₂, provide expanded information about crew conditions. Eight engineering indicators describe simulated environmental and operational conditions, including cabin atmosphere, pressure, temperature, humidity, radiation, and suit oxygen reserves.

The twelve additional indicators currently use separate rule-based screening rather than the five-channel CNN. This distinction allows HealthGuard to display broader mission information without misrepresenting the capabilities of its trained models.

Four independent fictional astronaut streams provide simulated monitoring data, while seven interactive scenarios reproduce different physiological, sensor, and environmental disturbances. Mission Control allows users to examine these changes, review monitoring responses, and investigate how mission conditions may influence the interpretation of physiological readings.

6. System Integration and Visualization

HealthGuard integrates its analytical components through a Python and FastAPI backend, which handles simulated telemetry, model inference, PhysioAlert assessments, and historical NASA biomedical research data. The trained CNN also has a lightweight NumPy inference implementation to reduce deployment requirements.

The frontend, developed using React, JavaScript, Vite, and Three.js-based visualization tools, presents the results through an interactive Mission Dashboard, Body Explorer, Health Library, Health Routine, Mission Control, and Mission HUD.

The Mission Dashboard displays simulated crew measurements and monitoring assessments. The Body Explorer connects physiological indicators with anatomical regions, while the Health Library provides educational information and access to historical NASA biomedical findings. Health Routine introduces interactive wellness activities, and Mission Control supports scenario exploration. The Mission HUD demonstrates how monitoring information could be presented within astronaut spacesuits during simulated Moon and Mars operations.

Through these components, HealthGuard brings personalized biomedical research, AI-assisted anomaly detection, contextual monitoring, and interactive mission simulation into one platform. The system maintains a distinction between authentic historical NASA laboratory data and simulated live measurements, supporting transparent interpretation of its findings and limitations.

How to Use It

HealthGuard was designed with an interactive, user-friendly interface that allows astronauts to examine physiological information, understand monitoring assessments, and explore health-related activities during simulated space missions. Users can access its features through the following steps:

1. Access the Mission Dashboard. Open the HealthGuard web application to access the Mission Dashboard, which provides an overview of the crew's simulated physiological conditions. The dashboard displays continuously updating measurements, physiological trends, monitoring indicators, and PhysioAlert assessments. Users can examine the available information and identify observations that may require additional attention.

2. Select an Astronaut and Monitor Physiological Indicators. Choose from four fictional astronaut profiles, each with an independent simulated telemetry stream. HealthGuard presents 17 physiological and engineering indicators, allowing users to examine vital signs and relevant spacecraft conditions. Interactive graphs help users explore measurement trends and observe how indicators change over time.

3. Review AI-Detected Anomalies and PhysioAlert Assessments. Access the monitoring details to examine unusual physiological patterns identified by the five-channel 1D-CNN autoencoder and covariance-based detector. PhysioAlert provides explanations based on detector agreement, physical activity, measurement quality, and anomaly persistence. Users can review these assessments to understand whether an observation may be related to exercise, unreliable measurements, or an unexplained physiological pattern requiring further investigation.

4. Explore Personalized Biomedical Analysis through APDRA. Open the Health Library to examine historical biomedical observations from NASA's Inspiration4 mission and explore the findings of Adaptive Personalized Deviation Reliability Analysis (APDRA). Users can investigate how preflight baseline measurements affect the interpretation of postflight physiological changes, helping them understand the importance of reliable personal reference data. This historical research component operates separately from the simulated live monitoring system.

5. Interact with the Body Explorer. Navigate to the interactive 3D Body Explorer to examine three anatomical regions and their relationships with physiological indicators. Users can select different regions to learn about relevant body systems, understand their functions, and explore how physiological changes may affect astronaut health during space missions.

6. Complete Gamified Health Routines. Access Health Routine to participate in interactive wellness activities, educational games, and daily health challenges. These include guided physical activities, health-related knowledge exercises, and progress-tracking features designed to encourage healthy habits and consistent participation. The activities demonstrate how astronauts could maintain structured wellness routines during long-duration missions.

7. Simulate Fictional Events through the Scenario Lab. Open the Scenario Lab to explore fictional events that demonstrate how astronaut health indicators may change under different conditions. Users can select simulated scenarios involving physical activity, physiological disturbances, sensor errors, and environmental hazards. Each scenario produces changes in the simulated telemetry, allowing users to observe physiological trends, examine AI-generated monitoring results, and understand how PhysioAlert responds to different patterns. These scenarios are intended for demonstration and educational purposes rather than representing actual astronaut medical emergencies.

8. Explore Moon and Mars Operations through the Mission HUD. Access the Mission HUD to examine how physiological indicators, spacesuit conditions, and mission alerts could appear inside an astronaut's helmet during extravehicular activities. Users can switch between simulated lunar and Martian environments and explore a transparent heads-up display designed to keep essential monitoring information visible while maintaining awareness of the surrounding environment.

Through these features, HealthGuard provides an integrated demonstration of astronaut health monitoring, personalized biomedical research, AI-assisted anomaly detection, and mission-oriented health education. The application uses simulated live telemetry alongside separately identified historical NASA biomedical observations. Its monitoring outputs are intended for research, education, and software demonstration rather than clinical diagnosis or operational medical decision-making.

Methodology and System Development

NASA Biomedical Data Collection and Preparation

We obtained historical biomedical measurements from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), specifically study OSD-575, which contains laboratory measurements from four astronauts who participated in the Inspiration4 mission.

The processed dataset consisted of 5,990 usable observations, including 509 Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) measurements covering 19 analytes and 5,481 Alamar NULISA measurements covering 203 protein targets. These records were organized by participant, biomarker, assay type, and collection timepoint, preserving the distinction between preflight and postflight measurements.

The dataset was used to investigate how changes in physiological biomarkers could be interpreted relative to individual reference measurements. Since these were historical laboratory observations rather than continuous sensor recordings, they were analyzed separately from HealthGuard's simulated real-time monitoring system.

Development and Evaluation of APDRA

We developed Adaptive Personalized Deviation Reliability Analysis (APDRA) to evaluate whether physiological screening findings remain consistent when individual baseline observations are excluded.

The framework applies a leave-one-baseline-out procedure, repeatedly recalculating an individual's reference median after removing one preflight measurement. Postflight observations are compared against these recalculated baselines to determine whether the detected changes remain consistent or depend on particular reference observations.

For CMP measurements, we applied an exploratory 30% absolute deviation threshold. NULISA protein measurements were evaluated using an absolute difference threshold of 1.0 on the log₂-normalized measurement scale.

APDRA was evaluated using the historical NASA dataset and controlled synthetic stress tests. The synthetic experiments compared APDRA with conventional median-based screening across 24 independent random seeds, two baseline-count conditions, and four noise configurations. Each experimental configuration included 3,000 calibration cases and 3,000 separate evaluation cases, allowing us to examine how baseline variability and measurement noise influence screening performance.

Development and Training of the 1D-CNN Autoencoder

For simulated continuous physiological monitoring, we developed a one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1D-CNN) autoencoder to identify unusual temporal patterns across five core indicators: heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), respiratory rate, body temperature, and heart rate variability (HRV).

The model was trained using 2,400 synthetically generated normal physiological episodes, representing variations in individual reference conditions and ordinary physiological fluctuations. An additional 480 normal episodes were used for threshold calibration.

Model evaluation involved 480 held-out normal episodes and 1,120 episodes containing injected numerical anomalies across seven disturbance conditions. These included multisignal shifts, oxygenation-related changes, temperature changes, autonomic-pattern disturbances, transient abnormalities, and gradual drift.

The model processes rolling 60-sample windows, normalized using an initial 45-sample individual reference period. It reconstructs the input sequences and calculates reconstruction error to identify patterns that differ from its learned normal simulated behavior.

The model was developed using Python and PyTorch, with a lightweight NumPy inference implementation prepared for deployment.

Development of the Covariance-Based Detector

To complement the CNN, we developed an independent shrinkage-covariance statistical detector that examines multivariable deviations across the same five physiological indicators.

The detector extracts 20 statistical features from each measurement window, including the mean, standard deviation, maximum absolute value, and beginning-to-end change of each signal. These features are compared against a learned reference distribution using a covariance-based novelty score.

The detector was trained using 1,800 synthetic normal episodes, with 400 additional episodes for calibration and 400 held-out normal episodes for evaluation.

The CNN and covariance detector use different numerical approaches, allowing HealthGuard to compare their findings and identify cases where the models agree or disagree about an unusual pattern.

Development of PhysioAlert

We developed PhysioAlert to interpret anomaly-detection results alongside relevant physiological and measurement context.

The framework evaluates four primary factors: detector agreement, declared physical activity, measurement quality, and anomaly persistence. It also checks for potential sensor problems, including missing measurements, irregular sampling, frozen signals, abrupt spikes, and spike-rebound patterns.

For persistent-pattern reviews, the implemented logic requires at least two qualifying positive detector checks separated by 15 seconds during declared rest. A separate 60-second post-activity observation period helps distinguish exercise-related changes from continued unusual patterns.

PhysioAlert generates understandable assessments such as Activity Context Review, Verify Measurement Quality, Detectors Disagree, and Persistent Pattern Review. Its behavior was examined through controlled synthetic telemetry replays to evaluate how the system responds to different activity and measurement conditions.

Expansion to 17-Channel Monitoring and Scenario Simulation

To provide broader physiological and mission-related information, HealthGuard's monitoring interface was expanded to 17 simulated indicators, consisting of nine physiological measures and eight spacecraft or spacesuit engineering measures.

The five core physiological indicators are processed by the evaluated CNN and covariance models. Four additional physiological measures, consisting of systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, skin temperature, and end-tidal CO₂, were incorporated alongside eight engineering measures covering cabin CO₂, oxygen concentration, pressure, temperature, humidity, radiation dose rate, accumulated radiation dose, and estimated suit oxygen reserves.

The twelve additional indicators use separate simulation-based screening rather than the original five-channel AI models. This preserves the distinction between trained anomaly-detection outputs and rule-based monitoring.

Four independent fictional astronaut telemetry streams were developed to demonstrate changes in simulated physiological conditions. The Scenario Lab provides seven fictional scenarios involving physical activity, physiological disturbances, sensor artifacts, and environmental hazards. These scenarios allow users to observe changing indicators and examine how the monitoring system responds under controlled simulated conditions.

Frontend Development and System Integration

HealthGuard's backend was implemented using Python, FastAPI, NumPy, and PyTorch for biomedical analysis, model development, simulated telemetry processing, and monitoring assessments. The frontend was developed using React, JavaScript, Vite, and Three.js-based visualization tools.

The application integrates several interactive modules: the Mission Dashboard for monitoring fictional crew members; Crew Telemetry for examining physiological trends; the Body Explorer for anatomical visualization; the Health Library for accessible health education and NASA biomedical research; Health Routine for gamified wellness activities; the Scenario Lab for demonstrating fictional physiological events; and the Mission HUD for exploring monitoring displays in simulated lunar and Martian environments.

Backend APIs and WebSocket-based updates support the presentation of simulated measurements and monitoring assessments. Docker and Render were used for application deployment, while GitHub supported source-code management and version control.

The platform maintains separate data pathways for historical NASA laboratory measurements and simulated live telemetry, ensuring that actual biomedical research observations are not presented as real-time astronaut sensor data.

Results and Performance Evaluation

HealthGuard was evaluated through historical NASA biomedical analysis, controlled AI anomaly-detection experiments, contextual monitoring simulations, and software testing. The results demonstrate the system's ability to assess the reliability of personalized physiological findings, identify unusual simulated patterns, interpret anomalies using contextual information, and integrate these capabilities into a functional monitoring platform.

APDRA Baseline-Sensitivity Analysis

Adaptive Personalized Deviation Reliability Analysis (APDRA) was evaluated using 5,990 historical biomedical observations from NASA's Inspiration4 mission. The analysis demonstrated the importance of examining the reliability of individual baseline measurements when interpreting physiological changes.

Among 195 postflight observations identified through conventional median-based screening, 68 observations (34.9%) were baseline-sensitive, meaning their screening conclusions changed depending on the reference measurements used. The remaining 127 observations (65.1%) remained consistent across the leave-one-baseline-out comparisons.

These findings demonstrate APDRA's ability to reveal baseline-dependent screening results that conventional single-reference comparisons may overlook, providing an additional layer of evidence assessment for personalized physiological monitoring.

In controlled synthetic experiments, APDRA also demonstrated improved injected-change detection compared with conventional median-based screening. It achieved improvements of 6.54 percentage points under two-baseline outlier conditions and 5.12 percentage points under three-baseline high-noise conditions, at approximately matched false-screen rates. These improvements were specific to the tested conditions, while the historical baseline-sensitive findings represent screening uncertainty rather than confirmed medical errors.

CNN Anomaly-Detection Performance

The five-channel 1D-CNN autoencoder demonstrated strong anomaly-detection performance during evaluation on held-out synthetic physiological data.

The model achieved a ROC AUC of 0.9812, indicating excellent discrimination between normal and injected-anomaly episodes within the controlled evaluation. It also maintained a 2.92% false-flag rate on held-out normal episodes.

The CNN successfully identified 100% of injected episodes across five tested disturbance categories, including multisignal shifts, oxygen-respiration disturbances, sustained temperature changes, autonomic-pattern changes, and short transients.

For more subtle disturbances, the model detected 83.75% of low-magnitude transient episodes and 48.75% of gradual-drift episodes. These results demonstrate strong recognition of pronounced simulated abnormalities while identifying gradual changes as an area for further improvement.

Overall, the evaluation supports the CNN's effectiveness in identifying unfamiliar numerical patterns in controlled simulated physiological data.

Covariance-Based Detection Performance

The independent shrinkage-covariance detector provided an additional statistical approach for identifying unusual physiological patterns.

It achieved a 71% detection rate for subtle-drift episodes in its synthetic evaluation, demonstrating its potential usefulness for examining gradual changes in multivariable physiological characteristics. The detector also recorded a 5.25% false-flag rate on held-out normal episodes.

By integrating covariance-based analysis alongside the CNN, HealthGuard provides complementary numerical perspectives on physiological anomalies. This allows the system to consider detector agreement and disagreement when generating monitoring assessments.

PhysioAlert Contextual Monitoring Evaluation

PhysioAlert was evaluated through four controlled end-to-end simulation scenarios involving physical activity, sensor artifacts, unexplained physiological disturbances, and normal conditions.

The evaluation processed 720 telemetry packets, producing 76 scored windows per scenario after initialization.

During declared physical activity, both anomaly detectors flagged all 76 scored windows. However, PhysioAlert classified 58 windows as activity-context reviews and 18 as post-activity observations, demonstrating how contextual information can influence the interpretation of unusual measurements.

During the sensor-artifact scenario, PhysioAlert identified 61 windows requiring measurement verification, showing its ability to recognize potentially unreliable readings and direct attention toward sensor quality.

In the unexplained physiological disturbance scenario, the system generated 76 contextual reviews, while the normal scenario demonstrated its ability to retain and report disagreements between the two detectors.

These findings demonstrate the successful integration of anomaly detection with activity awareness, measurement-quality assessment, and explainable monitoring responses.

Software Integration and Computational Performance

HealthGuard also demonstrated successful backend integration and computational efficiency.

The frozen HealthGuard backend passed 192 out of 192 automated software tests, covering computational functions, API operations, source separation, and system integration.

A local single-worker evaluation of the lightweight NumPy inference implementation recorded approximately 111 MiB of memory usage, supporting the feasibility of running the demonstrated monitoring backend with relatively modest computational resources.

The platform was subsequently expanded to include 17 simulated monitoring indicators, four independent fictional astronaut streams, interactive health education, the Scenario Lab, and Moon and Mars Mission HUD demonstrations. These additions broadened the functionality and accessibility of the prototype.

Based on these findings, HealthGuard is a promising AI-powered astronaut health monitoring tool that combines personalized biomedical analysis, deep-learning anomaly detection, and context-aware physiological monitoring. APDRA successfully identified baseline-sensitive findings using authentic NASA biomedical observations, while the 1D-CNN achieved a ROC AUC of 0.9812 and detected 100% of injected episodes across five tested disturbance categories in controlled synthetic evaluations. The covariance-based detector provided complementary anomaly analysis, while PhysioAlert demonstrated the value of incorporating physical activity, measurement reliability, and detector agreement into monitoring assessments. Furthermore, the successful completion of 192 automated backend tests supports the functionality and reliability of the evaluated software components. Although HealthGuard has not yet undergone clinical validation or testing with real-time astronaut physiological data, its analysis of authentic NASA biomedical datasets, strong performance in controlled synthetic experiments, and successful software evaluations demonstrate its potential for future real-world healthcare applications and long-duration space missions.

Innovation, Impact, and Applications

Compared with previous tools, HealthGuard offers a more comprehensive approach to astronaut health monitoring by integrating personalized biomedical analysis, AI-powered anomaly detection, and context-aware physiological assessment. While conventional monitoring systems often focus on identifying measurements outside predefined thresholds, HealthGuard also examines the reliability and context of the available evidence. Its Adaptive Personalized Deviation Reliability Analysis (APDRA) framework evaluates the consistency of individual baseline comparisons using historical NASA biomedical data, while a 1D-CNN autoencoder and covariance-based detector identify unusual patterns in simulated physiological signals. Through PhysioAlert, these findings are interpreted alongside physical activity, measurement quality, detector agreement, and anomaly persistence, providing more understandable monitoring assessments.

Beyond its analytical capabilities, HealthGuard combines 17 simulated physiological and engineering indicators with an interactive Mission Dashboard, 3D Body Explorer, Health Library, gamified Health Routine, Scenario Lab, and Moon and Mars Mission HUD demonstrations. These features allow users to visualize physiological trends, explore anatomical systems, understand monitoring results, participate in health-related activities, and observe how fictional mission events affect astronaut health indicators. By integrating scientific analysis with interactive monitoring and educational tools, HealthGuard makes complex physiological information more accessible and easier to interpret.

HealthGuard can be integrated and used for future lunar, Martian, and deep-space missions, where communication delays and limited medical resources may require greater astronaut independence. By supporting the recognition of unusual physiological patterns, identifying potentially unreliable measurements, and explaining why further assessment may be necessary, HealthGuard could contribute to preventive health monitoring, more informed decision-making, and improved astronaut safety. With further validation and hardware integration, HealthGuard could potentially support future lunar, Martian, and deep-space missions.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

ChatGPT (OpenAI) assisted with HealthGuard's research planning, algorithm development, programming, debugging, data analysis, software testing, interface design, and documentation, including work on APDRA, the 1D-CNN autoencoder, covariance-based detection, PhysioAlert, and the application's backend and frontend. The team directed development decisions and remains responsible for verifying the methodology, code, and results. HealthGuard's voice alerts use predefined scripts spoken through browser text-to-speech, while alarm tones are generated programmatically using the Web Audio API. These audio features do not use real-time generative AI.
